title: Applied anatomy: Calot's triangle and the biliary tree

guidelineVersions: Safe Cholecystectomy Multi-society Practice Guideline (Brunt et al., 2020)

brief.scenario: A 45-year-old woman is listed for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic gallstones. Written findings: a laparoscopic view during the cholecystectomy. The gallbladder fundus is retracted up over the liver and its neck is pulled laterally. The area bounded by the gallbladder neck, the main duct running down on its medial side and the inferior edge of the liver has been cleared of fat and fibrous tissue, so the liver can be seen through it. The lower third of the gallbladder has been separated from the liver bed. Two tubular structures, and only two, enter the gallbladder: a wider, lower one continuous with the gallbladder neck, and a thinner one above it.
brief.task: Using the written findings, answer the examiner's questions on Calot's triangle and the biliary tree, and explain how the anatomy is used to avoid bile duct injury.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Two triangles, one safe view, and what to do when you can't get it.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Giving the liver edge as the upper border of Calot's triangle. That is the hepatocystic triangle.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Calot's triangle is bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the cystic artery."

grid.label: The two triangles
grid.fail: Gives the wrong borders, or treats the two triangles as the same.
grid.pass: Calot's: cystic duct, common hepatic duct, cystic artery. Hepatocystic: cystic duct, common hepatic duct, inferior edge of the liver.
grid.high: Calot's usually lies within the hepatocystic triangle; the critical view clears the whole hepatocystic triangle.

grid.label: Contents
grid.fail: Lists the cystic duct as a content rather than a border.
grid.pass: Cystic artery and the cystic (Lund's) lymph node; the right hepatic artery may pass through.
grid.high: Uses the cystic node as a landmark for the nearby cystic artery; warns the right hepatic artery can loop close to the gallbladder.

grid.label: Biliary tree and variants
grid.fail: Cannot describe how the ducts join.
grid.pass: Right and left hepatic ducts form the common hepatic duct; the cystic duct joins to form the bile duct, which meets the pancreatic duct at the ampulla.
grid.high: Names variants that lead to injury: aberrant right hepatic duct, low or parallel cystic duct insertion, short cystic duct.

grid.label: Critical view of safety
grid.pass: Hepatocystic triangle cleared of fat and fibrous tissue; lower third of the gallbladder off the liver bed; two structures only entering the gallbladder.
grid.high: Pauses to confirm the critical view before clipping or cutting any duct or artery.

grid.label: When the view can't be achieved
grid.fail: Clips what looks like the cystic duct anyway.
grid.pass: Stops, calls a senior, uses cholangiography if the anatomy is unclear, and considers subtotal cholecystectomy or conversion.
grid.high: Prefers subtotal cholecystectomy to dissecting a hostile triangle, and explains why this avoids the bile duct.

grid.label: Bile duct injury
grid.fail: Plans to repair a major injury without hepatobiliary expertise.
grid.pass: Classic injury: bile duct mistaken for cystic duct and clipped. Presents with bile leak, jaundice or cholangitis.
grid.high: If recognised at operation, refers promptly to a hepatobiliary team rather than repairing; documents and follows duty of candour.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What are the borders of Calot's triangle?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the edge of the liver. It's the same as the hepatocystic triangle.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The cystic duct and the cystic artery.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How do the bile ducts join?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The hepatic duct runs into the gallbladder, and then into the duodenum.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What is the critical view of safety?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Seeing the cystic duct clearly before you clip it.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: You can't clear the triangle. What do you do?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd clip the structure that looks most like the cystic duct and carry on.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: You recognise you've divided the bile duct.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd try to join it back together over a T-tube.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What are the borders of Calot's triangle?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the cystic artery. The hepatocystic triangle has the same two ducts, but the inferior edge of the liver above.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The cystic artery and the cystic lymph node of Lund. The right hepatic artery may pass through it.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The right and left hepatic ducts form the common hepatic duct. The cystic duct joins it to form the bile duct, which meets the pancreatic duct at the ampulla in the second part of the duodenum.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What is the critical view of safety, and is it achieved here?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Three things: the hepatocystic triangle cleared of fat and fibrous tissue, the lower third of the gallbladder off the liver bed, and two structures only entering the gallbladder. All three are described in these findings.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd stop and call a senior. If the anatomy is unclear, a cholangiogram. Otherwise subtotal cholecystectomy or conversion.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What is the classic bile duct injury?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The bile duct is mistaken for the cystic duct and clipped and divided. It presents with a bile leak, jaundice or cholangitis.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Why do we talk about the hepatocystic triangle?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Calot's triangle usually lies within it. The critical view means clearing the whole hepatocystic triangle, not just the area below the artery.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The cystic node is a useful landmark, because the cystic artery usually lies close to it. I'd also watch for the right hepatic artery looping close to the gallbladder, where it can be mistaken for the cystic artery.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: An aberrant right hepatic duct, a low or parallel cystic duct insertion, and a short cystic duct. Each makes misidentification easier.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: You think you have the critical view.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd pause and confirm all three criteria before I clip or cut anything.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The triangle is scarred and you can't clear it.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A subtotal cholecystectomy. It removes the stone-bearing gallbladder without dissecting in the triangle, so the bile duct stays out of danger.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: You see you've cut the bile duct.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I wouldn't attempt a repair myself. I'd place a drain, refer promptly to a hepatobiliary team, document exactly what happened, and tell the patient under the duty of candour.

failures.move: Giving the liver edge as the upper border of Calot's triangle.
failures.consequence: Confuses the two triangles and the purpose of the critical view.

failures.move: Clipping a duct without the critical view.
failures.consequence: The mechanism of the classic bile duct injury.

failures.move: Attempting a repair without hepatobiliary expertise.
failures.consequence: Early non-specialist repair can worsen the outcome.

recovery.line: Calot's has the artery on top; the hepatocystic triangle has the liver edge.

recovery.when: Asked what to do when it's difficult
recovery.line: If I can't see the critical view, I don't clip: I stop and use a bailout.

knowledge.fact: Calot's triangle: cystic duct, common hepatic duct, cystic artery.
Hepatocystic triangle: cystic duct, common hepatic duct, inferior edge of liver.
Critical view: triangle cleared, lower third of gallbladder off the liver bed, two structures only.
Pause to confirm the critical view before clipping; cholangiography if anatomy uncertain.
No critical view: consider subtotal cholecystectomy. Recognised injury: refer promptly to an experienced hepatobiliary team.

recall.think: Misidentifying the bile duct as the cystic duct is how the classic injury happens.
do: State the three critical view criteria
recall.trap: Liver edge is the hepatocystic triangle, not Calot's.
recall.finish: Subtotal cholecystectomy when stuck; hepatobiliary referral for injury.

partner.opening: You have the written findings of a laparoscopic view during a cholecystectomy. What are the borders of Calot's triangle?

reveals.finding: Read out: a small, round lymph node lies within the cleared triangle. Ask: what is it, and why is it useful?
Say: now suppose the triangle is scarred and only one structure can be seen entering the gallbladder.

push.question: What are the borders of Calot's triangle, and how is the hepatocystic triangle different?
push.expect: Calot's: cystic duct, CHD, cystic artery. Hepatocystic: same ducts, inferior edge of liver.

push.question: Which variants increase the risk of injury?
push.expect: Aberrant right hepatic duct, low or parallel cystic duct, short cystic duct.

push.question: What is the critical view of safety?
push.expect: Triangle cleared, lower third off the liver bed, two structures only; pause before clipping.

push.question: What is the Strasberg classification?
push.expect: A: leak from cystic duct or small liver-bed ducts. B: occluded aberrant right duct. C: divided, unligated aberrant right duct. D: lateral injury to a major duct. E: circumferential injury of a major duct (E1–E5 by level).

curveballs.prompt: You can't achieve the critical view of safety. What now?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Do not clip. Call a senior, cholangiogram if unclear, subtotal cholecystectomy or conversion.

curveballs.prompt: Day 3, abdominal pain and a bile-stained drain. What is the likely cause?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Most often a cystic duct stump or liver-bed duct leak. Imaging, drain any collection, ERCP with stent; exclude a major duct injury.
